narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low academic standing in law school was the main reason the model saw a high risk of bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the second most important factor. Although it pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, the score still fell below the 37.2 average of accepted students, so it could not overcome the negative effect of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.0 was the third most important feature. Like the LSAT, it nudged the outcome modestly toward passing, yet it remained below the 3.23 average of successful applicants and was not strong enough to change the overall result.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class performance if you retake courses, or consider retaking the LSAT to achieve a noticeably higher score. Strengthening these academic signals will be the most effective way to shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
